analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $50 for a 30-day supply, including for the uninsured.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2021 and never received a vote or even a committee hearing; it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a $50 monthly out-of-pocket cap on insulin for people with private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, veterans' coverage, and TRICARE, and cap the cash price at $50 for uninsured people. Insurers and manufacturers would absorb the difference. The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 7 million-plus Americans who use insulin — diabetics with employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, VA or TRICARE coverage, and the uninsured — would pay at most $50 per 30-day supply instead of facing high deductibles and coinsurance, and anyone overcharged after 2022 would get reimbursed.

how_it_helps.text: No private health plan could impose deductibles, copays, or coinsurance on insulin that exceeds $50 per 30-day supply, regardless of how much insulin is prescribed. [S2, S3]
The same $50 cap applies to Medicare Part D, Medicaid, CHIP, VA, and TRICARE coverage. [S2, S3]
Uninsured people pay no more than $50 cash for a 30-day supply, and retroactive reimbursement covers anyone overcharged after January 1, 2022. [S2, S3]

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit plans would absorb the capped cost-sharing for insured enrollees, and insulin manufacturers would eat the capped cash price for the uninsured; federal health programs and the drug industry bear the cost of the government-plan caps.

drawbacks.text: The cap applies only to cost-sharing, not the underlying drug prices — manufacturers could still charge high list prices to insurers, keeping premiums and plan costs elevated. [S3]

Insurers might offset the mandate through higher premiums or reduced benefits elsewhere, and the bill lacks provisions addressing pharmacy benefit manager tactics like coinsurance-based formulary design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to insulin patients is substantial and the mandate is narrow, though it does not address root-cause drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced, read twice, referred to the Senate HELP Committee, and left there until the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Introduced April 15, 2021, read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. [S1, S5]
No further action; the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin users are no better off; insurers and manufacturers avoided the cap entirely, though none are named as blocking actors in the record — the bill simply languished without action or cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, no votes or recorded opposition — the bill died from inaction, not a fight.

industries.note: The bill caps what they can charge patients for insulin cost-sharing.
The bill caps the cash price for uninsured patients and mandates manufacturer reimbursement for overcharges.

industries.industry: Federal health programs (Medicare, Medicaid, VA, TRICARE)
industries.note: Capped cost-sharing reduces revenue but protects enrollees.
